name: Asbuilt — the living as-built record for Business Central and Acumatica implementations
one_liner: For the delivery lead at a 10-60 person Microsoft Dynamics 365 Business Central or Acumatica implementation partner, Asbuilt connects read-only to each client sandbox and production tenant, extracts the real configuration (setup records, configuration packages, extensions/customizations, roles, integrations), and turns it plus the project's own workshop notes into a client-ready as-built handover pack and a monthly change diff — the deliverable partners promise in the SOW and today write by hand in Word.
problem: Every mid-market ERP implementation ends with a promise: a handover pack that tells the client's new in-house admin what was configured and why. It is written by hand, late at night, by the functional consultant, in Word and Excel, from memory and meeting notes — then it is stale within a month because the partner keeps making changes under a support retainer. When it is missing or wrong, the client pays again: rescue/health-check engagements are quoted at roughly 40-80 hours at $150-$250/hr ($6k-$20k) and full remediation at $60k-$200k (business-software.com's published rescue analysis — an illustrative vendor calculation, not a survey), and NetSuite practitioners describe undocumented saved searches and month-end procedures as "tribal knowledge" that vanishes when the specialist leaves. On the NetSuite and Salesforce side this is a real, paid-for product category: Netwrix Strongpoint auto-documents customizations and dependencies (quote-based; third-party estimates $15k-$40k/yr), Salto does configuration management for Salesforce and NetSuite at $1.25/token/month (~$15k/yr for 1,000 tokens), Elements.cloud documents Salesforce orgs at $495-$995/month. For Business Central (40,000+ online customers per Microsoft; 55,000 companies on its product page) and Acumatica (10,000+ customers, vendor-reported), Netwrix's published coverage is NetSuite and Salesforce only, and I could not find an equivalent automatic as-built documentation product. Those ecosystems are served almost entirely by small partners with no tooling for the deliverable they contractually owe.
target_customer: The delivery/practice lead or managing partner at a 10-60 person Business Central or Acumatica VAR (the firms Microsoft and Acumatica sell exclusively through). They own utilisation and the fixed-fee overrun; documentation hours are the ones they write off. Buyer and user are close: the practice lead signs, the functional consultants use it. Secondary buyer later: the client's in-house ERP admin/controller who inherits the system and wants the record kept current under the support retainer.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Business Central's automation API now exposes configuration packages and installed extensions, and Acumatica's contract-based REST plus its customization API can retrieve customization-project content — so a third party can read enough of a tenant to draft an as-built without an on-prem agent (Microsoft Learn: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/business-central/dev-itpro/administration/itpro-introduction-to-automation-apis, Acumatica: https://beacon.acumatica.com/r/Integration-Development-Guide/Configuring-the-REST-API/Contract-Based-REST-API). (2) Long-context models make it cheap to turn a raw metadata dump plus messy workshop transcripts into readable, client-facing prose — the thing that was previously 100% human. (3) Business Central's 2026 wave 1 plan ships built-in agents and features for reviewing agent-generated content (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dynamics365/release-plan/2026wave1/smb/dynamics365-business-central/planned-features), which means the as-built must soon also record which agents are enabled, what they may touch and who approves them — a new chapter nobody's Word template has. This sits inside a16z's "Vertical AI evolves... to multiplayer" and "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" (Joe Schmidt, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-2/): the VAR channel is literally the forward-deployed layer for the 99%, and it has no tools. YC's Winter 2027 list has no direct match; I deliberately did not chase "AI for City Hall" or "Plaid for Government Benefits", which are far from this builder's skills.
comparables: Netwrix Strongpoint (https://netwrix.com/en/products/strongpoint/) — automatic customization inventory, dependency mapping and change records; published coverage is NetSuite and Salesforce only, quote-based pricing, one G2 reviewer says plainly "it's not cheap" and a third-party review says it isn't worth it for small teams with little customization. Gap: no Business Central, no Acumatica, and priced for the SOX-audit buyer, not the VAR. Salto (https://www.salto.io/pricing) — configuration management/diff/deploy for Salesforce and NetSuite, $1.25 per configuration token per month (1,000 tokens ≈ $15k/yr); gap: developer-facing config management, not a client-readable handover document, and again not BC/Acumatica. Elements.cloud ($495-$995/month, https://elements.cloud/salesforce-purchase/) — Salesforce org documentation tied to process maps; Salesforce-only. Sweep ($2,500-$7,000/month, https://www.sweep.io/pricing) — Salesforce agentic documentation workspace. superglue.ai (https://superglue.ai/, YC-backed, group-wide rollout across Pine Services Group's 18 ERP firms) — the most serious adjacent threat: an AI implementation platform covering discovery, design, configuration, testing/UAT and cutover across NetSuite, Sage, Dynamics, Acumatica; gap today is that it is a full-lifecycle platform aimed at the whole delivery motion and anchored on a signed design document, not a standing, always-current as-built record of the live tenant that survives after the project closes. Auctor ($20M led by Sequoia, https://www.getauctor.com/product) — same buyer (system integrators) but the front of the project: discovery calls to SOWs, scopes, user stories; it does not read the tenant. Catalio (https://catalio.ai/docs) — AI requirements discovery and configuration documentation for Salesforce/NetSuite; small, worth watching. Honest read: the gap is real but it is a narrowing one, and superglue is the reason this is a 7.2 and not an 8.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. Business Central: 40,000+ online customers (Microsoft) served by a partner-only channel; Acumatica: 10,000+ customers (vendor-reported), 100% channel. A plausible 1,500-3,000 BC/Acumatica implementation partners worldwide in the 10-60 person band. Perplexity's read on partner economics supports $500/month as an easy entry and $1,000-$2,000/month for a team-wide delivery tool; a 20-person partner running an estimated 10-30 project starts a year would be paying $200-$2,400 per project. At 300 partners × $1,200/month that is ~$4.3M ARR — a real seed-stage business, not a category-defining one, unless it expands into the client-side subscription (the in-house admin paying to keep the record live, which is where Strongpoint's $15k-$40k/yr NetSuite pricing shows the ceiling). Anchor price for willingness to pay: Strongpoint and Salto both clear $15k/yr for the same job on other platforms, and BC fixed-price implementation packages that explicitly include "documentation and handover" run $45k-$90k (bittaapps.com/pricing), so documentation is already inside a paid scope.
risks: Coverage trap: if the extraction only reaches 60% of what matters, the consultant still rewrites the document and the time saving evaporates. Channel sales are slow: VARs buy at user-group events and through peer referral, with long evaluation and small budgets — the first ten deals could take six months. Platform risk: Microsoft could fold "generate your handover doc" into Business Central Copilot for partners, exactly as it has been expanding partner AI tooling.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That the partner, not the end client, will pay — documentation is the deliverable partners most happily under-deliver, so the buyer may prefer to keep writing it badly for free rather than pay $1,200/month. This is the one that kills it; test it first. 2) That BC's automation API + custom API pages and Acumatica's REST/customization API expose enough of the effective configuration to produce something a consultant would send a client without heavy rewriting. Microsoft's own docs say the package endpoint is for package operations and status, not a full inventory of every effective setting — coverage, not API existence, is the risk. 3) That superglue.ai (YC-backed, already rolling out across 18 ERP firms) does not simply ship a better as-built module within two quarters and absorb this wedge.
first_customers: Ten named BC/Acumatica partners in the 10-60 person band, found three ways: (a) the Microsoft and Acumatica partner directories filtered by employee count; (b) Directions NA/EMEA and Acumatica Summit attendee and sponsor lists — these are where this channel actually meets; (c) the BC partner community on LinkedIn and the Dynamics subreddits, where delivery leads post about project overruns. Approach as a working consultant, not a vendor: "send me a sanitised sandbox and last project's handover doc, I'll return an as-built pack in 48 hours, free; if it saves you a day, we talk price." Start with firms that sell fixed-price implementation packages (they eat every documentation hour), e.g. the ones publishing $45k-$90k fixed-fee BC packages.
validation_test: This week: get three BC or Acumatica partner delivery leads on a call, ask each for one real (sanitised) client handover document and the hours booked to produce it. Then hand-build the as-built pack for one of them using only API reads plus a model — a weekend of work, no product. Pass: at least two of three say the generated pack is 70%+ of what they would have shipped, and one agrees in writing to a paid pilot at $500-$1,000/month for their next project. Fail: they say the document is mostly judgement and narrative that only the consultant who ran the workshops can write, or they shrug because the client never reads it — in which case the buyer is the client's in-house admin, not the partner, and the whole idea needs re-pointing.
build_plan: Stack: TypeScript + Next.js, a small Postgres, Claude/GPT via API for the prose layer. Narrowest first version — Business Central only, one partner, one project. 1) OAuth into a BC tenant (sandbox + production) read-only; pull configuration packages, installed extensions, permission sets/roles, company setup records and the custom API pages the partner exposes. 2) Normalise into a config model and store dated snapshots. 3) Accept the project's unstructured inputs: workshop transcripts, the SOW, the functional design doc, the issues list. 4) Generate the as-built pack — one chapter per business process (sales order to cash, purchase to pay, inventory, finance setup), each with: what was configured, the values, the extension/customization behind it, why (quoted from the workshop note), and who to call. Plus an explicit "we could not read these areas" coverage page — honesty is the trust feature. 5) Monthly re-pull producing a change diff: what moved since handover, with before/after. 6) Export to Word/PDF under the partner's logo. Cut for v1: Acumatica, NetSuite, Salesforce, any write access, deployment/migration, UAT script generation, agent governance, SOX workflows, approvals, multi-tenant admin. Resist building a platform; build one excellent document.
launch_post: Your ERP handover doc is written from memory at 11pm and stale in a month. Asbuilt reads the Business Central tenant, reads your workshop notes, and writes the as-built pack your client actually keeps — then diffs it every month. Partner-branded. BC first, Acumatica next.
reasoning: Tonight's bookmarks point twice at the same unglamorous place: the Auctor/YC post says the hardest part of enterprise software is translating business needs into something configurable, and the Grok Bot post shows a finance team formalising scope and ownership for every worker, human or bot. The crowded part of that is the front of the project (Auctor, $20M from Sequoia, sells discovery-to-SOW) and the middle (superglue.ai sells design, config, testing). The unglamorous step nobody owns is the end: the as-built record the client lives with for the next five years, and the diff that keeps it true while the partner keeps changing things under retainer. That step has a proven price on the neighbouring platforms — Strongpoint, Salto, Elements.cloud all charge $6k-$40k/yr for essentially this on NetSuite and Salesforce — and Netwrix's own published coverage says NetSuite and Salesforce only, which is as clean a statement of the gap as positioning ever gives you. Business Central (40,000+ online customers) and Acumatica (10,000+) are sold entirely through small VARs who have no equivalent tool. It beat the UAT-generator and cutover candidates because those are per-project purchases in territory superglue already occupies, and it beat the agent-governance candidates because the library already holds Shiftlog, Ledger and Doublecheck. It is a 7.2, not an 8: I could not find first-person partner complaints about writing handover docs (the evidence is vendor-side — rescue pricing, "tribal knowledge" articles, fixed-fee packages that bundle "documentation and handover"), and superglue.ai is a YC-backed company one product decision away from this wedge. The pain is expressed by the people who buy rescues, and only latent in the partner who should have prevented them — which is precisely why validation_test must start by asking a partner to pay, not by asking whether they agree it's a problem.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Asbuilt — as-built configuration record + monthly change diff for BC/Acumatica implementation partners. PICK. Only candidate where the incumbents' own coverage (Strongpoint = NetSuite/Salesforce only) draws the gap for me, and where a paid comparable price exists on the neighbouring platform.
2. Agent Payroll/HR for finance bots — onboard, scope and performance-review AI agents on an accounting team (from the Grok Bot post). DROPPED AT SCREEN as a near-repeat of Shiftlog (18 Nov) — same controller buyer, same agent-evidence workflow; also BlackLine's Finance Control Console with OpenAI (17 Nov 2026) lands exactly here.
3. Cutover command centre for mid-market ERP go-lives — the Saturday-night runbook in Excel. FINALIST, lost. Cutover.com and Enov8 exist but aim at banks; the real killer is frequency: a partner does this a handful of times a year, so it is a per-project purchase with no weekly pain.
4. UAT script generator from a configured sandbox — generate business-user test scripts from what was actually configured. FINALIST, lost. superglue.ai explicitly generates implementation test scripts and runs sandbox tests for partners; LogicHive sells the UAT workspace at £45-£649/month. Too directly occupied, and the price point is low.
5. Hypercare triage agent — reads the flood of post-go-live user emails and routes/answers them for the partner's support desk. Dropped at screen: 8-week window per project, blurs into generic helpdesk AI (Intercom/Zendesk), no durable wedge.
6. Data migration reconciliation — prove legacy balances tie out to the new ERP before go-live. Dropped at screen: real pain and a genuinely narrow step, but it is one weekend per project and partners already have Excel tie-out sheets they trust more than a vendor.
7. Mobile approval inbox for agent actions in back-office systems (from the DigitalOcean Cuttlefish post, applied to finance not devs). Dropped at screen: overlaps Shiftlog/Doublecheck/Ledger in the library and is a feature of every agent platform.
8. Benefits document wallet — verify income/household once, reuse across programs (YC "Plaid for Government Benefits" signal). Dropped at screen: strong signal, but the buyer is a state agency with an 18-month procurement cycle and incumbents (Truv, Argyle) already sell government income verification. Wrong shape for an evenings-and-weekends solo builder.
9. Permit correction-letter automation (YC "AI for City Hall" signal). DROPPED AS REPEAT — Backcheck (28 Oct) is the same buyer and workflow.
10. First-month-close copilot for companies that just went live on a new ERP — the controller's worst month. Dropped at screen: the buyer is in crisis and will pay for a human, not software; one-off, no retention.
11. Data-centre long-lead equipment expediting (YC "Data Center Supply Chain" signal). DROPPED AS REPEAT — Slotkeeper (7 Nov).

PROJECT
1. Roster — paste your job title, get the bot team that would do it, from Anthropic's robot-exposure task data. PICK: personal input, evidence-backed output, built to post, data refreshes.
2. Payslip-for-the-whole-team — weekly cost card for all your running agents. Dropped at generate: near-repeat of past idea Payslip.
3. Agent Remote — open-source phone console to approve/stop agents on a remote box (from @KlausCodes' question + DigitalOcean Cuttlefish). Dropped at screen: Paperclip, OpenHands Agent Canvas, Agent Orchestrator and Antigravity Mobile all already do this; crowded and needs a real backend.
4. Untangle Score — paste a repo, get a "mess score" (copy-paste, leaky abstractions, useless wrappers). Dropped at screen: clone-adjacent to @mazeincoding's /untangle-codebase and overlaps three past repo-analysis ideas (Blindspot, Ghostwritten, Surrender).
5. Mac Cluster Card — visualise a local k8s cluster from Apple container 1.7.1. Dropped at screen: audience is tiny, output is a boring diagram, nothing to share.
6. Gate — turn a plain-English chore ("chase unpaid invoices") into a structured bot spec with scope, sources of truth and approval gates. Finalist: research found no clean free generator, but the output is a wall of YAML — low shareability, and it's a thin wrapper on one prompt. Folded its best part (approval gates) into Roster.
7. Geofence — one sentence becomes a location-based reminder shortcut (from @trq212). Dropped at screen: needs a phone app or Shortcuts export, can't be a static page, and iOS already does geofenced reminders.
8. Meeting Artifact Museum — a public gallery of artifacts Claude Meetings generates. Dropped at generate: no API confirmed (checked), and it's content, not a tool.
9. First Mutual Fund — a one-screen jargon-free explainer for first-time investors (from @misbahspeaks). Dropped at screen: regulated, regional, and the builder has no edge here.
10. Demo Dog — recreate Auctor's "dog photo that booked hundreds of demos" as a cold-outreach image generator. Dropped at generate: gimmick with no second use, and borderline spam-enabling.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the x.ai Grok Bot accounting post (five bots own provisioning, billing, billing support, cash application, collections; invoice processing 24h→minutes, reconciliation 3-4h→~30min, all self-reported), Auctor (sells to system integrators, $20M led by Sequoia Apr 2026, drafts SOWs/user stories from discovery calls — this is what told me the front of the project is taken), and DigitalOcean's Cuttlefish (mobile approve/deny for agent tool calls — useful context, but it pushed candidate 7 toward "this is a feature"). Screening pot (6/6): O2C agent market (HighRadius, Stuut, Fazeshift, Monk — dense, killed candidate 2); ERP UAT/spreadsheets; SOX/ITGC change evidence; hypercare; cutover tooling (Cutover.com is bank-shaped, quote-only); YC "Plaid for Government Benefits" (Truv and others already there). Deep research (12/12): Cutover.com pricing and customer profile; Reddit consultant complaints on NetSuite documentation and traceability; the as-built tool landscape with real prices (Elements.cloud $495-$995/mo, Salto $1.25/token/mo ≈ $15k/yr per 1,000 tokens, Sweep $2,500-$7,000/mo); partner-economics sizing; UAT tooling (Panaya, Original Software, Opkey, superglue, LogicHive at £45-£649/mo); superglue.ai's full scope and Pine Services Group rollout — this is what forced me off the UAT candidate; Salesforce Metadata API vs NetSuite System Notes feasibility; Strongpoint pricing and G2 complaints ("it's not cheap", not worth it for small low-customization teams); NetSuite rescue economics ($6k-$20k health checks, $60k-$200k remediation). Sharpening pot (5/5): spent confirming the reshape — that Strongpoint's published coverage is NetSuite/Salesforce only, that BC has 40,000+ online customers and Acumatica 10,000+, that BC's automation API exposes configuration packages and extensions and Acumatica's REST/customization API can retrieve customization projects (feasible but coverage-limited, which is now an explicit product feature), that BC partners already bundle "documentation and handover" in $45k-$90k fixed-fee packages, and that BC 2026 wave 1 ships agents plus agent-content review (the new chapter in the as-built). Investor signals weighed: a16z "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" and "Vertical AI... to multiplayer" (the VAR channel is the forward-deployed layer); YC "AI for City Hall" and "Plaid for Government Benefits" considered and rejected as repeats or wrong-shape for this builder; YC "Data Center Supply Chain" rejected as a repeat of Slotkeeper.
Sharpening (6.6 to 7.2): Round 1 — weakest criteria: gap (6) and market_pull (6). The original shape was "AI as-built documentation for ERP implementations", platform-agnostic. Research showed that on NetSuite and Salesforce the gap is largely closed: Netwrix Strongpoint auto-documents customizations and dependencies, Salto does config management at ~$15k/yr, Elements.cloud at $495-$995/month, Sweep at $2,500-$7,000/month. Change made: narrow the platform to Business Central and Acumatica, the two volume mid-market ERPs sold only through small VARs. Evidence: Netwrix's own published product page lists coverage as NetSuite and Salesforce only; I found no equivalent automatic as-built product for BC or Acumatica; BC has 40,000+ online customers (Microsoft) and Acumatica 10,000+ (vendor-reported). Incumbents' own positioning draws the boundary, which is the 9-anchor condition for gap. gap 6 → 7.5, market_pull 6 → 7 (named buyer, and a proven $6k-$40k/yr price for the same job on neighbouring platforms, though I have no BC/Acumatica partner saying out loud that they'd pay).
Round 2 — weakest remaining: timing (6) and wedge (6.5). Change made: anchor the product on the live-tenant APIs rather than on documents, and add the agent chapter. Evidence found: BC's automation API exposes configuration packages and installed extensions and Acumatica's contract-based REST plus customization API can retrieve customization-project content (so read-only extraction is feasible for a solo builder) — but Microsoft's docs also say the package endpoint is for package operations and status, not a full inventory of effective settings, so coverage is genuinely partial. That cut both ways: timing 6 → 7 (APIs plus BC 2026 wave 1 shipping agents and agent-content review, a documented dated change), wedge 6.5 → 7 (a weekend can produce a hand-made pack for one partner, but a sellable product is months, and the coverage gap means the consultant still edits — so no 8). I also tried to raise pain above 7.5 and could not: the rescue-cost numbers ($6k-$20k health checks, $60k-$200k remediation, the $25k-$60k reverse-engineering figure) are all vendor-published estimates, and I found no independent first-person partner complaint about writing handover docs. Held at 7.5. Average before sharpening 6.6, after 7.2.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): Perplexity summaries of Apple container 1.7.1 cluster docs (confirmed experimental local k8s on Mac — real but a niche, unshareable output), the x.ai Grok Bot accounting post (gave me the five named bots, their scopes and the explicit human-approval gates — this shaped Roster's output format), and Claude Meetings (confirmed no Meetings API, killing candidate 8).
Screening pot (5/5): searched for an existing codebase-mess visualiser (nothing clean, but clone risk), remote agent control dashboards (found Paperclip, OpenHands Agent Canvas, Agent Orchestrator, Antigravity Mobile → killed candidate 3), bot org-chart generators (nothing), job-description→AI-task-split tools (surfaced the Anthropic robot exposure index, which became the backbone of the pick), and geofence/location-reminder tools.
Deep research pot (8/8): confirmed the Anthropic EconomicIndex robot_exposure release is real, public, CC BY 4.0, 923 occupation rows and 18,796 task rows with exposure_tier, reasoning, instances and cited sources; confirmed the sources field carries real robot evidence with maturity/autonomy metadata (so evidence chips are honest); checked prior art — Washington Post's paywalled 2026 lookup, JobRoute's enterprise O*NET scoring, Eraser's org-chart generator, Grok Bot community "Team Builder" templates — none combine job → named bots → scopes → gates → human column; confirmed Grok Bot's own docs now frame bots as having a job, sources and approval boundaries; confirmed the March 2025 automation_vs_augmentation_by_task.csv covers knowledge-work tasks the robot file marks non-physical. What changed: the pick moved from "AI exposure score" (crowded, doom-y) to "staffing plan with a human column" (fresh, postable).
Sharpening pot (2/4, both used): dataset refresh cadence (lifted usefulness) and the 99.5 MB file size + CORS/licence check (forced the offline-ETL build plan, lifted buildability). Two sharpening calls left unspent — the remaining weak spot is unverified: I have no direct evidence that people will return weekly rather than look up their job once.
Sharpening (7.6 to 8.2): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (5, a one-time toy: you look up your job once and leave). Change: added the "Only you" column as a first-class output (the card is as much about what stays human as what a bot takes), plus a weekly "This week" page of most-looked-up occupations and any task whose exposure tier changed when Anthropic refreshes the index. Research (Perplexity on the EconomicIndex dataset) confirmed the index is a recurring release — the robot exposure file landed 30 Sep 2026, the AEI "Cadences" report 26 Jun 2026 — so "the data changes" is real, not invented, which makes a weekly re-check honest. Usefulness 5 → 7 (capped below 8: I could not verify a fixed refresh cadence for the robot file specifically). Score 7.6 → 8.0.
Round 2 — weak criterion: buildability (7, unchecked data path). Change: moved all heavy data work offline into an ETL step shipping a pre-reduced JSON, after research showed `robot_exposure_tasks.csv` is 99.5 MB with 18,796 rows and the sources field holds nested JSON — far too heavy for a browser fetch, and CORS on the HF resolve URL is unverified. Licence checked: CC BY 4.0, commercial web reuse allowed with attribution and the USDOL/ETA non-endorsement note. Buildability 7 → 8 (not 9: the JD→SOC matching path still needs a model call and one tiny serverless function). Score 8.0 → 8.2.
prototype_summary: An interactive three-pane prototype showing a messy Business Central implementation's raw artefacts being turned into a generated, source-linked as-built document pack with a November change diff and export toast.
